segments.text: Mr Speaker, on behalf of the Congress Party—Poovaraghan, pardon me—on behalf of the Syndicate Congress Party, one no-confidence motion has been placed before this House; and on behalf of the other parties, particularly under the leadership of the Left Communist Party, a censure motion has also been placed. Thirty-six members have expressed all their views on those motions.

A no-confidence motion was brought here once before by our Leader of the Opposition. At that time they were fifty in number. After they moved a no-confidence motion against us, eight of them left, in effect saying that they had no confidence in them. Now the principal opposition, the Congress Party, has forty-two members remaining. To the extent that the present no-confidence motion serves to demonstrate that they have no confidence in us, it equally gives us the opportunity to demonstrate that this State and the majority of the members of this House do have confidence in us—and will have even greater confidence in us. It gives us the opportunity to explain the reasons for that confidence.
When individual criticisms are voiced outside, at public meetings and elsewhere, we may not be present there to refute them or give direct explanations.

In such circumstances any number of accusations can be made. But when all of them are debated face to face and we are able to give direct explanations, the four crore people of Tamil Nadu get an opportunity to understand the truth. In that sense I am happy that the no-confidence motion is, in one way, useful to us.

The parties that have brought the censure motion have strongly criticised us, this Government, and particularly the conduct of the police functioning under the authority of this Government. I understand that the Left Communist Party, the Right Communist Party, the PSP and the SSP have moved this censure motion with the good intention that this Government should bring about further improvements in the police, prevent even some of the unfortunate incidents that arise in unavoidable circumstances, and thereby strengthen the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam Government as a Government with a left-oriented outlook. I therefore have no intention of simply rejecting them or speaking in vehement condemnation of them.

As for the no-confidence motion, if we ask whether, as the leader of the new Congress, Poovaraghan, has said, they attacked our policies, our programmes of action, or mistakes in the work programmes we have framed—the answer is no. Most of the attacks from the opposition under this motion have concerned individual ministers, alleged favours, car-presentation functions and matters of that kind. We in this House know that very well.

Whenever such allegations have been published, the ministers responsible have risen and given appropriate explanations. Those explanations have appeared in newspapers that believe in observing journalistic duty. There may be a few publications that say, in effect: “We do not care about journalistic ethics. Somehow the DMK must be brought into disrepute. Are these the people who should rule? Who are they? Ordinary people, common people—people not born into high-status families regarded as fit to rule; people from backward and oppressed conditions; representatives of communities kept in subjection for generations—are they now to adorn the seat of power?” Such angry publications may have suppressed the explanations we gave from time to time. I do not wish to attack even them. In the language taught to us by Anna, who made us rulers, I am obliged to say: “Long live they too.”

Members of the ruling party have brought out so many important facts and supplied such firm answers that neither I nor the ministers have had to answer every accusation ourselves. As leader of the ruling party in this Assembly, I must congratulate those members who argued with such ability.

At the same time I offer my heartfelt thanks to the Congress members who spoke on the no-confidence motion with dignity and without damaging the traditions of this House, and to members of other parties who, even though they did not support both motions, took part in the debate on the censure motion with a firm belief that the traditions of the House must be preserved.

The mere fact that the opposition declares that it has no confidence does not mean that the people of Tamil Nadu outside will say that they have no confidence in us. Even our Leader of the Opposition, speaking in the Assembly on 7 March 1970, said: “In other States coalition governments are formed and suddenly collapse; there is uncertainty about who will form the ministry. Here there is one government, a stable government. I cannot but appreciate that.” I know very well that they have moved this no-confidence motion with the good confidence that the stable government will continue. I therefore trust that they will not withdraw that appreciation.

After the DMK assumed office there are many measures by which we can judge whether the people and voters of Tamil Nadu have shown affection and confidence toward this party and toward the parties allied with it. Six or seven months after we assumed office came the South Madras parliamentary by-election, caused by Arignar Anna vacating that seat. It was said that the people had somehow mistakenly voted for us before and that this time they would defeat us. But the DMK candidate in that by-election received an overwhelming number of votes and won a major victory.
That victory, in the sixth month, was evidence of the confidence the people had in the DMK.

Then came the Tenkasi by-election. Although it had been a Congress seat and although the DMK candidate had earlier lost there by 500 votes, in the later by-election the DMK won by roughly 20,000 votes. That was because of the confidence people placed in the movement and in its Government. Then came the Sattur by-election. The DMK supported an allied party there, and that ally, the Swatantra Party, won. Everyone knows this. Nor can anyone forget that after we assumed office, the DMK won sufficient seats in the Corporation to take responsibility there. In municipal elections there had previously been only seven or eight such places; now DMK chairmen preside over more than fifty municipal councils. These are signs of popular confidence in this Government.

It is also true that there was once a time in Pondicherry when we could not even recover our election deposit. But after the DMK Government came to power here, elections in Pondicherry led to a coalition of the DMK and the Right Communist Party, with a DMK man becoming Chief Minister. The pleasant breeze created by the good functioning of the DMK Government in Tamil Nadu reached Pondicherry too; that is why the movement achieved such a victory there.

The Leader of the Opposition spoke about Panchayat Union elections, saying that lists and false figures were being produced and that these were not party-based elections. My respectful request is that he take the newspapers of both parties and examine them date by date. When elections for panchayat chairmen were held, which papers first proclaimed “Congress victory, Congress victory”—Congress papers or DMK papers? Let him examine that.

Only after such reports appeared did DMK publications face the necessity of publishing comparable figures. In the Panchayat Union chairman elections the DMK secured 178 places. Eight or ten may have been independents elected with DMK support. Congress repeatedly said it was untrue that 178 had won and that our claim was false. The people nevertheless understood the position. Now they have even issued a statement through Ram Subhag Singh. In two days the Panchayat Union chairmen are to be introduced at the State Autonomy Conference. I do not know whether even then they will believe it or say that we have substituted other people and that these are not the real chairmen.
Thus the Panchayat Union elections have clearly demonstrated that the people have confidence in this Government. During the debate on the censure motion much was said about police firing.

My dear friend Karuthiruman, the Leader of the Opposition, said that police repression had crossed all limits. I shall give the figures available to me for the twenty years of Congress rule; if more information is gathered the figure will only rise, not fall: 108 instances of police firing. According to that Government's own figures, 155 people were killed. A party under whose rule there were 108 firings and 155 deaths cannot now sit in the opposition and say that firing has gone beyond limits under the DMK Government.

Communist members may ask: “If Congress did it, does that mean you too can do it?” I therefore refer also to Kerala under Communist governments. Under Comrade E. M. S. Namboodiripad, from July 1958 to July 1959, there were four firings and nineteen deaths. In Kerala between 1967 and 1970 there were fifteen firings and nineteen deaths. I do not deny that police firing has taken place under the DMK Government. It has. But it occurred under circumstances considered unavoidable, and whenever it happened those of us in government were shocked. We must not forget that in earlier times governments could answer, in effect, “If people go where firing is taking place, what else can be done but shoot?”

blocks.text: Even after their demands were fulfilled!

segments.text: Many agitations took place. Members spoke about labour. In earlier times agitations followed the rejection of workers' demands. The curious thing here is that some of the agitations began only after this Government had considered the workers' demands, accepted their representations, completed negotiations and fulfilled those demands.

Take the Electricity Board employees. When they asked for advancement in service, I held discussions with them for four or five days. The minister concerned, I as Chairman of the Board, and the trade-union representatives all sat together. Wages that had not been raised for ten or fifteen years were raised to an extent that imposed an additional burden of about four crore rupees on the Electricity Board. The engineers shook my hand, thanked me and left. Yet within two days—I do not know why—they suddenly announced a strike. Not all employees, but the engineers.

They said the strike would begin at midnight. But at five in the evening itself they stopped work, in such a way that electric lights went out even in cities, and they left the machinery in a condition in which no one could immediately restart it. When reporters asked whether the Government would simply watch such a conspiracy, I said that this Government would not permit conspiratorial acts and would suppress such conspiracies with an iron hand. They then removed the words “conspiracy” and held on only to the words “iron hand.”

I had said that if conspiracies occurred we would suppress them with an iron hand. But the earlier words were discarded and “iron hand” alone was repeated: farmers' agitation—iron hand; land-seizure movement—iron hand; whatever the agitation—iron hand. For some time the phrase became very common in political discussion. But what action did we actually take? Action was taken against nine people; nine were arrested. When they gave written assurances and returned to work, all nine were pardoned and taken back. None was victimised; the Board did not engage in retaliation.

This matter must be viewed with compassion. Electricity is a public issue and an essential need. Because a strike in such a service was considered dangerous, they were arrested—but every arrested person was released. The incident, for political reasons, was staged only after wage increases worth about four crore rupees had been given and their demands accepted. This must be acknowledged with fairness.

Similarly at Neyveli, the workers met me before launching an agitation. I was then suffering severe eye pain. We sat together for three or four days, and an arrangement was reached that produced roughly ninety-two lakh rupees in wage increases. They celebrated May Day on 1 May, but because of certain doubts that arose that day, they struck work the next day. Later they themselves admitted that the strike was illegal and that they had not given the statutory notice.

Some untoward incidents connected with the strike led to police firing, and Deva Anbu died. Everyone in this Government expressed deep sorrow and sympathy. We did not pat the police on the back and say, “You agitated, Devanbu was shot—good.” Without anyone demanding it, we instituted an inquiry. The inquiry report itself faulted an officer for entering the settlement, and action has been taken against him. I tell this House that we will accept the inquiry report.

As for the Coimbatore farmers' agitation, the Government knows their demands and their difficulties. Mr Poovaraghan spoke to me about them. Because he had himself served as a minister, I explained the difficulties involved. Representatives of the farmers' association led by Mr Manradiyar came to us and we announced a decision. The Leader of the Opposition later said in this very House, in effect: even if you have crossed half the well, cross the whole well. I did not refuse to consider the farmers' problem. The subsidy itself involved several crores of rupees. We said that wells above seventy-five feet would be charged nine paise and the others ten paise. The association's secretary wrote thanking us for the concession but said that wells below seventy-five feet constituted only fifteen per cent in Coimbatore district, while eighty-five per cent benefited at nine paise, and asked that the remaining fifteen per cent also be charged nine paise.

I told them that we could not fix nine paise for their district alone, because similar reductions would then have to be made in other districts, causing the Government to lose several more crores, and asked them to wait. Yet within a day or two a statement was issued saying that they would launch a violent agitation. Later they themselves wrote that such language had been wrong, but the agitation took place. News came that three persons had been killed by bullets. This is not a Government that says it does not matter even if three or thirty die. We did not treat it as a prestige issue. Once we knew that three lives had been taken by bullets, an inquiry was ordered even before anyone could demand one. Compensation was offered; it was refused, or people were made to refuse it.

The Government offered compensation without waiting for a demand. We felt sympathy and recognised that firing had occurred under circumstances considered unavoidable. When I say 'Congress rule,' Mr Karuthiruman may think I mean Bhaktavatsalam. But one must ask whether Congress rule from the period of the respected Kamarajar onward had a record of acting with that same feeling.
It was said that the police used repression in the land-seizure movement. The Communists will become angry as soon as I call it a land-seizure movement; they call it a land-recovery movement.

They planned to conduct this movement across India and announced that they would conduct it in Tamil Nadu too. Before it began, strong statements appeared challenging: “Let us see what Karunanidhi's iron hand does.”

They announced that the movement would begin on the 15th—15 August, the day India attained independence, the day India was recovered from the British. On that day they planned to seize land from landlords. A march was organised, and the police understood that it was not merely for propaganda but to recruit people locally for land occupations. The police therefore watched closely and acted. Even in those actions Communist leaders were not treated without dignity. I instructed prison officials that they must not be subjected to unnecessary inconvenience.

blocks.text: Special facilities for a Communist leader

segments.text: Mr Kalyanasundaram and Mr Manali Kandasami were already in poor health. Mr Kalyanasundaram had respiratory illness and even in the Assembly found it difficult to stand and speak; at public meetings he generally spoke sitting down. Manali Kandasami was also unwell. I instructed that special care be taken. When it was said that he should be brought from Tiruchi to Madras, I said: do not bring him in a police lorry as I was once taken to Palayamkottai; bring him by car. He was brought in a senior police officer's large car and admitted to a hospital in Madras.
He was properly cared for.

That was not all. Communist friends involved in the movement who had to contest Panchayat or Panchayat Union chairmanship elections, or had to vote in them, could have been kept in prison if this Government had wanted to prevent them from participating. Instead, because we believe in democracy, we released all those who needed to participate. They took part in the elections. No one lost a Union chairman election merely because he had been arrested or imprisoned; in the places they had targeted, they did win.
I respectfully ask our Communist friends, as friends and allies, to consider what methods were used and how the police behaved when similar movements took place in Kerala.

When the new land-reform law came into force in Kerala on 1 January, Left Communists occupied land and put up huts; a Communist government arrested them on the 2nd. On 4 January Kerala police removed 700 huts erected on poramboke land in Alappuzha district. Imagine the photographs that would have appeared in newspapers had that happened here. On 3 January, in Thiruvaniyoor in Ernakulam district, police used lathis during an agitation by Marxist occupiers.
Seven persons were seriously injured.

On 5 February employees of the Kerala Road Transport Corporation struck work; 1,300 persons were arrested under the Achutha Menon Government. What did Achutha Menon say? He said that because of unfortunate incidents the police had been compelled in some places to use lathis and firearms, and that if a political party called for violence and led it, no government could simply stand by. That was said in Kerala by a leader of the Right Communist Party.

Yet here our Right Communist friends ask whether people engaged in violence may be restrained or suppressed. In addition, settlers fenced off ten cents each and took ten cents of land each. How did that Communist Government respond? Fifty thousand cases were registered. Here it was said that ten thousand persons had been arrested; Mr Nallasivam said there were perhaps three thousand more from other groups. Whatever the exact count, they proudly spoke of ten thousand. But the Right Communist Government in Kerala filed fifty thousand cases, 1,200 people were subjected to police action, and 200 were beaten in police camps. I remind my Communist friends that these facts were published by the newspaper *Theekkathir* on 23 August 1970.
You say that exemptions have not all been abolished in Tamil Nadu and that the DMK Government is running alongside the landlords. You tell ordinary people that exemptions must be abolished.

But what is the truth? I ask what the position was in Kerala under both Left Communist and Right Communist administrations. There were exemptions under the ceiling law for the lands of temples, mutts and mosques; private forests; factory lands; estates; and public trusts. Therefore it is not proper to say that only here you are conducting this agitation because exemptions exist. I remind you of this even though the agitation has now ended.

blocks.text: We order judicial inquiries and seek remedies

segments.text: Consider whether, during the three to three-and-a-half years of this Government, appropriate action has or has not been taken whenever police action occurred during agitations. The Keezhvenmani incident was terrible. When it happened, all of us saw Arignar Anna remain without food or sleep for two days. Mr Ramamurthi, MP, who spoke with him, saw how exhausted and grief-stricken he was.

It is even said that Keezhvenmani was somehow a DMK incident. When Congress brought a censure motion, Mr Sankarayya said he could not support it because Congress had brought it for political advantage and that the Communists opposed such use of the tragedy. I remember his words clearly.
He himself recalled them at the time.

Therefore no one should use the Venmani tragedy for political profit. It was an unexpected tragedy. The Ganapathi Pillai Commission was appointed to study how peace could be established in Thanjavur district. We did not say that what happened at Keezhvenmani was over and remain idle. We immediately examined the problem and sought ways of creating peace in the Thanjavur region. On the Commission's recommendations fair wages were fixed, and all of you know that a more peaceful situation now exists in the district.

There are many examples showing that this Government has not hesitated to order judicial inquiries into police firing. An inquiry into the Aravankadu firing was entrusted to District Judge Ganesan, who submitted a report.

When clashes occurred in Madras between students and bus workers, Justice Somasundaram conducted an inquiry. Acting on his recommendations, compensation amounting to thousands of rupees was paid to affected students.
An inquiry into the Udayarpalayam firing was entrusted to Justice Ramaprasad Rao.
For Perumanallur, former High Court judge Ramakrishnan, GCS, was appointed to conduct the inquiry.

But I ask you to remember another event: the Mudukulathur violence of 1957, over which a major no-confidence motion was moved and the House itself shook with debate. How many bodies floated in the fields? How many children fell into burning haystacks? How many women were widowed? I do not want to divide people as Thevars and Harijans. They were people of this society, citizens of Tamil Nadu. A river of blood ran through Mudukulathur. For forty days there was such brutality that one could not distinguish whether what lay upon the crops was water or blood. Five Maravars were tied and blindfolded at a temple entrance, lined up before the police, and, at the command to fire, counted one, two, three, four, five—one man shot at each count.

Five members of the Maravar community thus lost their lives. Adi Dravidar people were thrown into haystacks and burned; they were murdered. What did we ask for? When Communist leader Kalyanasundaram and Perarignar Anna demanded a judicial inquiry, did the Kamaraj Government agree? Kamaraj was seated here then. What did Mr Subramaniam seated beside him say? He said that if there were judicial inquiries into everything, the police would no longer even lift their guns and would not be able to perform their duty.

blocks.text: Was there a judicial inquiry into Mudukulathur?

segments.text: We order judicial inquiries now. But for that forty-day upheaval and bloodshed—
was an inquiry ordered into the Mudukulathur tragedy? I remind the House that the Congress ministry under Kamaraj failed to do so.

**Karuthiruman:** I was the ruling party whip then. A no-confidence motion was moved. Did the DMK support that motion? I ask whether the Chief Minister, who is now arguing so strongly on their behalf, could not have supported it and voted for it then. They did not.

**Chief Minister:** I asked whether there was a judicial inquiry. Anna showed generosity because the motion was directed specifically against Kamaraj and said: “I am not prepared to accept it; therefore I shall remain neutral on the no-confidence motion.” But in his concluding speech he demanded a judicial inquiry. When I ask why you did not hold that inquiry, Mr Karuthiruman asks why we did not vote for the motion. I am speaking about the absence of an inquiry.

**Karuthiruman:** If you truly wanted a proper judicial inquiry you should have voted for the no-confidence motion. What position did they take? They said whoever was responsible, whether there was disorder or mistakes by the Government, it should be prevented. Today they sympathise with Achutha Menon and others; my question is why they did not vote for the no-confidence motion then.
**Chief Minister:** I request the Leader of the Opposition to read all the Assembly proceedings—to see what Arignar Anna said and when he walked out.

I am pressing the point behind the censure motion. What I asked was this: whether the dead were Thevars or poor Harijans, a judicial inquiry was demanded on behalf of the dead and was not granted. That is my charge, nothing more. Firings may occur, depending on circumstances; mistakes may occur. The difference is between a government that said in effect, “Yes, that is how we will act,” and a government that says, “Alas, this has happened; let us hold a judicial inquiry.” That is the distinction I ask you to recognise.

Deaths in police custody were also mentioned. I have repeatedly taken a severe view of such conduct by the police. We condemned lock-up deaths when we were in opposition and we condemn them now that we are in government. Did we issue an order after coming to power permitting people to die in lock-ups? On the contrary, as Mr Sankarayya himself recalled, we ordered that an arrested woman should not immediately be kept in a police lock-up but should be sent to a sub-jail.
In the Ayla Ammal case, police officers are under suspension and are no longer on duty. In Mayavaram, a man named Raghavan died; an inquiry was immediately conducted, and when fault was found,
the police officer was suspended.

So when a person dies in a lock-up this Government does not merely invent a story that he died naturally or committed suicide. Of course someone may genuinely die naturally, or in some cases may hang himself. But when cruelty is actually involved, severe action is taken. Whatever the circumstances, this Government does not ignore allegations; it investigates the facts. The Raghavan case at Mayavaram and the Ayla Ammal case in Thanjavur are two recent examples.

The Leader of the Opposition then spoke about the Amathur incident. According to the information I received, at about 9 p.m. on 7 February, an Harijan named Kattu Karuppan, while sleeping at the village chavadi, was attacked with an aruval and killed. Karuppannan, his son Ayyavu and his wife Karuppayi were accused, but the Ramanathapuram Sessions Judge acquitted them. Both the deceased and the accused belonged to the Harijan community. The deceased was a registered habitual offender who had previously been punished sixteen times. The District Superintendent of Police has reported that no Harijan was killed at Amathur merely because he bought a house in an area inhabited by caste Hindus.
If the Leader of the Opposition can provide further reliable information I am prepared to have it investigated and to take action.
I shall now answer some smaller charges before coming to the larger ones.

It was alleged that MLAs were holding car-presentation functions. Between 1967 and 1970 the Government allotted 159 cars: 100 to DMK members, 28 to Congress members, seven to the Swatantra Party, five to the Praja Socialist Party, three to the Left Communists, two to the Tamil Arasu Kazhagam, one to K. P. S. Mani of the Republican Party, one to A. K. Subbaiah of the Right Communist Party, and five to independents.
**V. K. Kothandaraman:** Nobody in our party bought a car.
**Chief Minister:** I said “allotment.” If you do not want to buy one, do not. That is a different matter.
**V. K. Kothandaraman:** You said they had bought them.
**Chief Minister:** I explained how allotments were made. Allotments are made on request; they are not simply imposed without anyone asking.
Another allegation was that cars were sold without permission. Fifteen MLAs have sought permission to resell. Even Congress member Vinayagam sought permission.
**K. Vinayagam:** I have not sold mine; I still have it. Go outside and see it. *(Laughter.)*
**Chief Minister:** He sought permission. I mention even Vinayagam precisely to protect you from the allegation that cars were sold without permission.
**K. Vinayagam:** The question now is about gifts.

**Chief Minister:** Cars are bought with money contributed by the public. Even a car for Thiruverumbur Swaminathan was presented from public contributions through Kamaraj. Some people cannot buy cars themselves. Some MLAs may be wealthy and buy cars with their own money; many on our side are poor and ordinary people, so the public collect money and buy cars for them.
Then it was said that some officials remain in the same place too long.

**Karuthiruman:** Some remain in certain places for a long time while others are frequently transferred. That is why administration is not functioning properly. It is not enough to point to four or five people who stayed long; some are moved repeatedly and sometimes return to the same place after leave. That was my point.

**Chief Minister:** You referred to the Nilgiris Collector, who has remained there for four years. One reason is the presence of Naxalbari-related activity requiring continuous monitoring. Another is the accumulation of knowledge concerning encroachment on Government lands; if a new Collector were posted, that experience would be lost. Therefore he has not been transferred. But was there no history of officers serving more than three years under your Government? There is a long list.
Congress governments too kept district collectors in one place for more than three years.

Vedanarayanan remained in Thanjavur from 1962 to 1966, four years. Sokkalingam, IAS, was Collector at Tiruchi from 1962 to 1967. Ambashankar remained in Kanyakumari for three and a half years. Ghulam Muhammad Basha remained in Tiruchi for four years. Prabhakar, IAS, served four years in Ramanathapuram-Madurai. Apart from these, between 1960 and 1967 under Congress, many police officers remained in the same post for more than three years. There were about ten such officers; over the relevant period, roughly nineteen officers in the Congress administration served more than three years in one place. Under this administration only seven have done so. This accusation is hardly momentous and is certainly not a sufficient basis for a no-confidence motion. Mr Karuthiruman himself will recognise it as a minor charge among many.

Then the Cooum river scheme was discussed. Dr Hande too appears to have spoken after reading a newspaper report. The history given by the Chief Engineer was that the British had contemplated such a scheme seventy or eighty years earlier but gave it up as impracticable; after independence a scheme of about 114 lakh rupees was drawn up, made executable by 1962, and ultimately taken up in 1968-69. Former Congress member R. Krishnaswami Naidu said in the Legislative Council that it was a good scheme that should be completed.

We said the Cooum should cease to stink. The Leader of the Opposition emphatically said, “The Cooum stinks, it stinks.” That depends on one's nose. *(Laughter.)* Does anyone want the old stench of the Cooum to remain forever? Should the river be improved or not? Only the mosquitoes that have lived there for generations could oppose its improvement.

Then came allegations of corruption in the Cooum scheme, corruption in the Veeranam scheme—“corruption everywhere, corruption in everything; bring the files.” A newspaper had written sensationally that because of a terrible smell of corruption the DMK Government had decided to abandon the Cooum improvement scheme; that work was ordered to stop until January; and that a scheme first put at Rs 1.36 crore would rise toward Rs 2 crore and was a vast storehouse of corruption. Dr Hande should not base his charge merely on such a report. It is false that the Government decided to abandon the Cooum scheme.
The works already taken up are proceeding according to plan and under supervision.
It is not true that Government ordered Cooum work to stop until January. The estimate is Rs 1.10 crore; it is not true that it will grow to Rs 2 crore.

Even now five or six hundred labourers are working vigorously in the river. Because of rain, a few slabs along the banks fell and there were breaches in one or two places. It is false propaganda to say that two or three crores have therefore been spent. Our project was Rs 1.10 crore, and so far only Rs 81 lakh has been spent.
Calling everything “Cooum corruption” is simply part of their political rhetoric.

blocks.text: The fate of the Vidur dam

segments.text: If you speak in this manner about the Cooum scheme, what happened to the Vidur reservoir scheme constructed during your rule? Built in 1959 at a cost of Rs 89 lakh, it breached in the rains of 1966 and another Rs 22 lakh had to be spent on repairs. The breach deposited sand over twenty or thirty acres, and this new Government has paid many thousands of rupees in compensation to the owners of those lands.

Yet because two concrete slabs somewhere along the Cooum slipped in the rain, you say the Cooum “stinks.” We undertake projects; occasionally mistakes occur. That does not make the entire scheme corrupt. The Vidur reservoir itself did not last even five or six years without such failure.

**K. Ramamurthi (Congress):** Mr Speaker, the Vidur reservoir did not fail because of a defect in the scheme. It failed because of a mistake by the engineer supervising it. *(Laughter from the ruling benches.)*

**Chief Minister:** Next, Mr K. Vinayagam spoke sharply about the Veeranam project, and Minister Sadiq Basha replied. I believe a detailed answer to the charges regarding Veeranam will be useful to this House.

Three firms stated in their tenders that they would use prestressed concrete pipes manufactured by the centrifugal process. Such pipes are known to be strong, durable and resistant to rapid deterioration under water pressure, and have been used widely in water-conveyance schemes.

Among the tenders, three firms proposed one method and two proposed vertical casting. The so-called vacuum process is used principally to remove water from concrete and assist curing. The name “vacuum” arises from that process; it does not imply an entirely different kind of pipe.

Removing water this way allows pipes to be taken from their moulds sooner, and tests have shown that such pipes can be 11 to 48 per cent stronger. It is therefore wrong to claim that only centrifugally produced pipes are strong and durable or that only those are used throughout the world. Vacuum-process pipes are also used in many water-conveyance schemes and have been in use for years in Iran, Sardinia and Greece.
Pipes of diameters larger than those required by us are made by this method in Tehran and Sardinia. Experts say that the vertical method can be used for large-diameter pipes.
Both methods are acceptable. Our foreign study tour showed that pipes made by both methods have given satisfactory service.
The next question was: what amounts were quoted by the other firms, why were they not accepted, and what was the difference between the successful tender and the rejected ones?
The tender we accepted was Rs 1.24 crore below the next tender—a very substantial difference. The pipes to be supplied by the lowest tenderer are of high quality and strength.
They are durable, and there need be no doubt about that. Certificates from Rome and Tehran support this, as did the report of our team that toured abroad.

Another allegation is that Government negotiated only with the lowest tenderer and ignored the quality and longevity of the centrifugal pipes proposed by higher tenderers. The answer is that the proper procedure is to negotiate with the lowest tenderer. Until the lowest tender is rejected, negotiating with other tenderers would itself be objectionable and contrary to procedure. There was no fault in the process we followed.

It was also alleged that during negotiations the lowest tenderer agreed to reduce the foreign-exchange requirement from about Rs 180 lakh to Rs 120 lakh, on condition that Government add Rs 90 lakh to its tender of about Rs 15.60 crore. That is substantially true.

The lowest tenderer, Sathyanarayana Brothers, had originally sought about Rs 181 lakh in foreign exchange for equipment, machinery, moulds, rubber rings and technical expertise needed for manufacture.

The Central Government, while approving the Veeranam drinking-water project, stipulated that the foreign-exchange component should be reduced as far as possible, even if that raised the tender price by up to twenty-five per cent.

Accordingly Sathyanarayana Brothers were asked to reduce the foreign-exchange requirement. They said they could reduce it to Rs 120 lakh, but asked for an additional Rs 90 lakh in the rupee component. Their reason was that steel, machinery, vehicles such as lorries and tractors, and other equipment that had originally been expected from abroad would instead have to be bought within India, and domestic purchase would cost more. This was examined. There is indeed a large price difference between importing steel and buying it domestically.

For example, steel rods bought in India cost about Rs 4,000 per ton and are not always available in the quantities required; imports could cost about Rs 1,800 per ton. Steel plates and other materials too cost more when sourced domestically. This is why the requested increase was considered.
We agreed to the additional Rs 90 lakh, while the foreign-exchange requirement was reduced by Rs 60 lakh—a desirable reduction.
You asked what the other tenderers quoted and how much foreign exchange they sought. I will give those details.

blocks.text: Why were the other tenders not accepted?

segments.text: Indian Hume Pipe Company: tender Rs 17,79,17,785; foreign exchange Rs 80 lakh.
Kerala Prema Pipe Company: tender Rs 18,57,47,674; no foreign exchange.
Sathyanarayana Brothers: tender Rs 16,55,87,300; foreign exchange Rs 1,20,00,000.
Tarapur & Company: tender Rs 18,60,07,009; foreign exchange Rs 1,50,00,000.
Universal Piping Construction: tender Rs 21,02,24,327; foreign exchange Rs 80,95,374.
Neelakandan Brothers: tender Rs 23,03,94,156; no foreign exchange requested.
Engineering Construction Corporation: tender Rs 12,64,85,844. Excluding the price of steel plates, for the pipes alone they sought Rs 40,00,000 in foreign exchange.
Stewarts & Lloyds: Rs 52,44,000 for rings alone; no foreign exchange.
After hearing all this, you yourselves can judge which tender we could reasonably have selected.

Another allegation was that the difference between the lowest tender and the next tender was only a few lakhs. I have already shown that this is wrong: the difference was about one and a quarter crore, a substantial amount. I have also said that adequate certificates establish the strength of the vacuum-process pipes.

Then it was asked why the contract was given to a complete newcomer. Sathyanarayana Brothers are neither people specially favoured by us nor newcomers. During the earlier Congress administration itself they received contracts worth crores: about six crores for various quarters at Avadi, a fifty-lakh job for the Small Arms Project, about fifty lakh for the Royapuram RSRM Hospital, grain godowns in Madras and Tiruchi and many other works—about forty-five works worth roughly twenty-one crore rupees—which they completed.

If, instead of the roughly sixteen-crore tender of Sathyanarayana Brothers, we had awarded the work to Tarapur & Company whose bid exceeded eighteen crores, what would you have said? You would have asked why Tarapur was chosen when a lower bidder existed and cited earlier High Court criticism of Tarapur. So the lowest tender was accepted. The contractor had already completed many works and possessed experience. There is no special relationship between him and us.
I have thus answered the major allegations generally raised. Ministers will answer other matters as necessary.
Mr Sankarayya spoke about achievements for labour. Although much of his speech criticised the police, he also said that the DMK Government's labour policy was not correct.
In 1969 alone, the Electricity Board and Public Works Department provided employment to 430 persons.

blocks.text: Labour policy of the DMK Government

segments.text: Through the employment exchanges, jobs were obtained for 44,875 persons in 1967, 41,581 in 1968 and 42,770 in 1969. Among them were 5,024 diploma holders, 2,315 engineering graduates and 8,739 persons trained in trades.

Of thirty-five closed industrial units, this Government reopened seventeen in 1969; four were taken over by the Tamil Nadu Textile Corporation. About ten thousand persons thereby obtained employment. This itself shows that the DMK Government is a workers' government. Our policy is: let industry grow, let the worker prosper; workers, Government and employers should resolve grievances through negotiation.
As a symbol that this is a workers' Government, the DMK Government made May Day a compulsory paid holiday.
Mr Sankarayya said the Government suppresses labour struggles and sides with capitalists.

But when employers themselves threatened lockouts or stoppages, this Government did not simply accept their demands. It enacted emergency legislation preventing them from stopping work. Mr Sankarayya's own conscience will tell him that this Government does not merely side with employers.

In industrial matters this Government does not display a vaidika—an orthodox—mentality. Industry must grow and expand. Private capital invests; Government invests; we also want a joint sector combining the two. When we say this, we are mocked for inviting industrialists and Minister Madhavan is accused of going north to court them. I remind Mr Sankarayya that E. M. S., of his own party, invited Birla to come to his State and establish industry. If E. M. S. invited Birla, it was to develop industry and employment in his State. Efforts to attract industry and jobs should not be mocked merely in the name of ideological rigidity; they should be appreciated.
Nor is that all. Even Communist Russia invited the Fiat car company to establish automobile production. In a country that speaks of socialism, a private Fiat company was invited to produce cars.
So I remind you that even there production takes place through a private-sector firm.

The Leader of the Opposition accused the Government of doing nothing for farmers, students, teachers or non-gazetted officers. Those who spoke after him repeated the charge. Time does not permit every detail, so I shall mention a few.

Food production, which stood at 57.6 lakh tonnes in 1967-68, increased again by 1969-70 despite the terrible drought in between. Because of this we abolished food controls. The Leader of the Opposition called that a political stunt and predicted that controls would soon return. I replied that if necessity required it, we would restore them without making it a prestige issue. By God's grace, that necessity has not arisen.
**K. Vinayagam:** Do you believe in that?
**Chief Minister:** Do not be afraid. God left your side a long time ago. The issue is not whether we accept God; the issue is whether God accepts us.
**Karuthiruman:** That is God's problem.
**Chief Minister:** The issue is not whether God accepts us or we accept God. We act in a manner that God can accept. We saw as early as 1967 that He did not accept you.
Through land-development banks, greater credit assistance is now being provided.

Previously loans were generally given only where the assessed value was Rs 10,000 or more; we changed the rule so that those with property worth Rs 5,000 could also obtain loans. Credit is extended up to about seventy-five per cent after assessing likely agricultural returns.
Through cooperative irrigation organisations, small landholders are being brought together so that irrigation facilities can be provided cooperatively.

Even during the drought roughly Rs 18 crore was spent. About 13,400 small and large irrigation tanks and their channels were desilted; 5,500 road works were undertaken; 683 soil-conservation works and 821 kudimaramathu works were carried out; 34,625 wells across the State were deepened and new wells dug. At one time more than eight lakh rural people were provided employment through these works.

Mr Vinayagam said we had done nothing for students. Compensation was paid for losses suffered by students during the student-bus-worker disturbances. When law-college students asked that even those who had not passed the first-year B.L. examination be allowed to continue into the second year, this Government accepted their request without obstruction or hesitation. The demand relating to the semester system in engineering colleges was also considered.

Only the day before yesterday I discussed the problems of house surgeons with them for more than an hour, and as many of their demands as possible were accepted. When oppressed-category students came with demands and officials behaved harshly, their grievances too were taken up for consideration.

We have extended free education up to the pre-university level. For backward-class students the minimum marks required for scholarships and assistance were reduced from fifty per cent to forty-five per cent. For the most backward classes the threshold was reduced from forty-five to forty per cent. This will cost the Government an additional two crore rupees.

Whenever dearness allowance was given to others it was extended to teachers. City compensatory allowance was extended to grant-aided school teachers; house-rent allowance was extended to local-body school teachers; and grant-aided school teachers were given earned-leave facilities.

Rules were framed to give permanent teachers earned leave, a concession not previously available. Each year higher-grade posts are being converted into secondary-grade posts so as to increase employment opportunities. About 5,000 teachers benefited in 1967-68, 3,000 in 1968-69 and 3,000 in 1969-70.
Under the earlier pension arrangement a cut-off date in 1955 meant that only those retiring after that date were covered.
Teachers who had retired earlier were disadvantaged. In 1968 the new Government extended pension benefits to teachers who had retired before the 1955 date.

The family-pension scheme was extended after 1 April 1969 to teachers in the private sector as well. P.T. and secondary-grade teachers acquiring higher qualifications such as B.A., B.T. or M.A./M.Litt. became eligible for two advance increments under a scheme introduced by this Government.

The Government has given the relevant allowances to non-gazetted officers and appointed a pay-review committee. It has decided to replace the old secret confidential-report system for Government employees with a more open record system. It introduced advances to Government servants for the marriages of their sons and daughters.
Government employees have been permitted to draw from provident funds to attend evening law-college classes.

For Government servants drawing more than Rs 250 a month, Government rental housing units were built in the Pattinapakkam Peters Road settlement. At the request of lower-division clerks, their designation was changed to “Junior Assistant.” A Police Commission has been appointed for police welfare.
A commission has been formed to study the welfare of backward classes, and a second pay commission has been constituted.
Its recommendations are awaited shortly.
The Government is intensively planning and implementing a programme so that by 1972 Tamil Nadu should not remain without electricity.
Drinking-water schemes costing about twenty crore rupees have also been taken up and work is proceeding.

It is said that we do everything only for our own party. Under Congress in 1966 a scheme was introduced to provide freedom fighters Rs 50 per month. If, after coming to power, we had thought only of our own people, we could have changed the law and restricted assistance to those who had participated in the anti-Hindi agitation from the DMK.
But as heirs to Arignar Anna's tradition we did not do that. In 1966 the total paid to freedom fighters was only Rs 3,057, covering 107 persons in the year.

After the DMK came to power, expenditure rose to about Rs 11.11 lakh in 1967-68, Rs 24.16 lakh in 1968-69 and Rs 32.67 lakh in 1969-70; for 1970-71 an estimate of about Rs 35.04 lakh was being considered. Assistance now reached 6,002 persons, including Congress freedom fighters.
We also granted Namakkal poet Ramalingam Pillai Rs 200 per month.
When he recently said that amount was insufficient and asked for Rs 250, the increase too was sanctioned.
Similarly we are providing assistance to Parali Nellaiyappar. We are also assisting five members of the family of Kattabomman.

They ask, “What have you achieved?” Is obtaining the Salem Steel Plant not an achievement? It may have been conceived during Congress rule, and I am obliged to thank Mr Venkataraman, Mr Subramaniam, who was Finance Minister, and Mr Kamaraj for their contributions. But when the project had not materialised, was it not our effort that helped bring it? Tuticorin, once only a fishing harbour, was developed as a deep-sea harbour. During our period the DMK and allied parties conducted an “Ezhuchi Naal” agitation; did the Tuticorin fertiliser factory not follow? Did we not secure an additional second-stage 200-megawatt development at Kalpakkam?

The Food Minister now gives another example. A long-pending request for a Murrah buffalo farm at Alamathi has received Central approval, with about Rs 82.91 lakh over four years. Will you not accept this too as an achievement of the DMK Government?

Does all this mean we are completely satisfied? No. Much more remains to be done. Our argument, and that of Tamil Arasu Kazhagam leader Silambu Selvar M. P. Sivagnanam, is that the powers presently available to the State are insufficient. When we ask for powers, why do you say “Do not give them”? Why say “Do not give money” for drought relief? When we seek powers, why play the role of Sukracharya blocking the gift? I use a story from mythology only as an illustration; examples are a familiar art to us too. Why stand in the way and say “Do not give, do not give”? The road is blocked—move a little aside, child. When we ask for powers, we ask them not only for ourselves but for you, for future generations, and for the four-and-a-half crore people of Tamil Nadu.

You speak about the demand for a separate State flag. These materials have come from Malaya. Look: Malaysia has fewer people than Tamil Nadu. The letter from Malaysia says that, with land area only somewhat greater than Tamil Nadu's and a population only a fraction of Tamil Nadu's, their small country has thirteen States. Each is roughly the size of a Tamil Nadu district; each has its own chief minister and ministers, its own legislature, its own flag and its own emblem.
There is also a separate flag and emblem for the central federation—the national flag and national symbol. These flags I show you were not printed here; they came from Malaysia.

Seemaisamy, speaking angrily, said, ‘If from now on you support Indira Gandhi, we will not remain with you,’ and said that he had spoken only after obtaining Rajaji's permission. Rajaji too has commented. With great humility I ask Seemaisamy, as the Swatantra Party leader here, and I ask the elder leader Rajaji as well. There are two hundred princes. For the sole ‘offence,’ as printed here, of saying that grants should be given to those princes, having said ‘we will not join M.K.,’ Rajaji now joins the Syndicate. I ask Rajaji: will he join the Syndicate that voted against the life, language, rights, prosperity and future of four-and-a-half crore Tamil people? We and the left parties supported Mrs Indira Gandhi there in saying that grants should not be given to the two hundred princes. Was that right or wrong? I ask Rajaji to think about it not once but twice.

The no-confidence motion brought by our friend Karuthiruman is not one that this House can properly accept. Perhaps, after hearing these explanations and these achievements, he may in a generous spirit choose to withdraw it.

The Left Communist Party and the other parties in the left alliance spoke about the police. The views expressed by them, and also those expressed by people such as Mr Poovaraghan, will be examined and appropriate action taken. I therefore request Mr Sankarayya too to withdraw the censure motion.
